[← All posts](../../index.qmd)

You have your gennaker up and it turns out you can juuuust about lay the next mark while being on the cusp of wiping out. The jib would maybe be almost as fast but you continue anyway - peeling is for whimps. Well is this really the fastest way? Is sailing lower and faster and then switching to the jib in the end to sail much higher to lay the mark better?

Lets get unnecessarily detailed here. Lets start with a fictive polar diagram of a boat with a jib and gennaker. The gennaker is responsible for the part of the polar in the down wind section and the jib is reponsible for the part in the up wind section. At some point they intersect and the sails are equally quick. That is usually around the time where we decide to switch. Let's assume we want to go somewhere that calls for a TWA just at that crossover. This is shown in Figure 1.

![The jib and gennaker polars meet at 115.49° TWA, our desired direction. Both sails give 8.28 knots there. [Open full size](sail-change-crossover-intro.svg).](sail-change-crossover-intro.svg){.compact-figure fig-alt="Blue jib and brown gennaker polars overlap. A green dashed ray marks the desired direction through their crossover at 115.49 degrees TWA. A green dot marks the shared speed of 8.28 knots. No bridge or sailing modes are drawn."}

But there is a conspicuous dent in the combined polar near that crossover. We could sail lower and faster under gennaker for part of the leg, then change to jib and sail higher to lay the mark.

The idea is to find the two sail-and-TWA combinations that make this route as fast as possible. We call those optimal combinations *modes*. Sailing part of the leg in one and the rest in the other is sailing *between modes*.

We still need to show that combining two such choices can beat sailing directly, and find which choices are optimal. The polar diagram gives us a way to do both, even in steady wind.

## Straight lines give an equivalent polar

Each point on a sail's polar describes a possible heading and boat speed. Pick two points and spend part of the time sailing at each. Distances add, so the horizontal and vertical speeds on the polar diagram average in the same proportions. Both coordinates vary linearly with the time fraction, so the possible averages trace the straight segment joining the points. Half the time in each gives its midpoint; other time splits give the rest of the segment.

To find the fastest combination, choose the outermost bridge across the dent that touches both curves while keeping all available points on the origin side. At smooth contact points, the bridge is tangent to each curve. **Its contact points identify the modes**: the optimal sail-and-TWA combinations to use on the two parts of the leg.

![The desired direction passes through the jib-gennaker crossover. The red bridge joins modes G and J, giving 1.15 knots more average speed toward the mark. [Open full size](sail-change-between-sails.svg).](sail-change-between-sails.svg){.compact-figure fig-alt="Overlapping blue jib and brown gennaker polars. The mark-direction ray passes through their crossover at 115.49 degrees TWA and 8.28 knots. A red bridge joins J at 94.54 degrees to G at 122 degrees. P A lies on the bridge at 9.44 knots, a 13.90 percent gain."}

The bridge lies outside the sail polars between G and J. Its radius in the mark direction therefore gives a greater average speed toward the mark than either sail gives when sailing directly there. This is why these two modes are worth combining. No wind shift is needed. It is the same idea as tacking or gybing, now between reaching modes.

Together with the exposed parts of the original curves, the outer bridges form a convex boundary, the **convex hull**. This is an equivalent polar for routes that can combine modes. Where the boundary follows a sail curve, sail directly; where it follows a bridge, combine its endpoint modes.

## The bridge points give the laylines

For the red bridge, the two modes are:

| Mode | TWA | Boat speed |
|---|---:|---:|
| G: gennaker | 122.00° | 10.33 kn |
| J: jib | 94.54° | 7.95 kn |

These are the layline angles for the two modes. They generally differ from the sail-polar crossover, which only compares the two sails at the same heading.

Draw the jib layline backwards from the mark, at the J heading plus 180°. Sail mode G until reaching that line, then change sail and head directly to the mark in mode J. In steady wind, reversing the order gives the same total time.

Changing the mark direction within this sector changes how long each mode is used, while the two endpoint modes stay fixed. The mark ray meets the bridge at $P_{\mathrm A}$. The distance from J to $P_{\mathrm A}$, divided by the full length JG, gives the fraction of time spent under gennaker.

Here the mark is at the crossover, **115.49° TWA**, where both sails give **8.28 knots** directly toward it. For these polars, this is the worst direct-sailing case within the bridge sector. Switching sails while staying on that heading gives no improvement. We use the gennaker for the direct boat.

The bridge puts 70.8% of the time in G: about **4:15 under gennaker and 1:45 under jib**. The average speed toward the mark becomes **9.44 knots**, a **13.90%** gain. The route is slightly longer, 0.96 rather than 0.94 nautical miles, but takes **6:00 instead of 6:50**.

## Two boats from A to B

Both boats start at A and sail to B. The direct boat holds the gennaker on the crossover heading. The modes boat sails G first, then changes to J at the backward layline from B.

![Combining modes reaches B in 6:00 instead of 6:50, saving 50 seconds. Colour shows each boat's lead at equal elapsed times, in Seascape 27 lengths. [Open full size](sail-change-crossover-leg.svg).](sail-change-crossover-leg.svg){fig-alt="A single leg from A to B at the jib-gennaker crossover angle. The direct boat uses the gennaker throughout, at the same speed the jib would give. The modes boat sails below the direct course under gennaker, then heads up under jib to reach B sooner. An inset compares both positions when the modes boat finishes."}

The construction assumes constant wind, settled speed, and no losses when changing mode. A real sail change has to cost less than the time saved. But being able to lay the mark, even with the faster sail for that heading, does not by itself make the direct course quickest.
